claims.text: High levels of lattice distortion enhance hardness and strength in high-entropy alloys.
Lattice distortion creates local stress fields that inhibit dislocation motion.
Inhibited dislocation motion raises the barrier to plastic deformation relative to alloys with less lattice distortion.
The proposed comparison is restricted to single-phase high-entropy alloys with comparable microstructures and minimal pre-existing defects.
Selecting constituent elements with larger differences in atomic radii will systematically increase lattice distortion while equiatomic balance is maintained.
Identical heat treatments can provide sufficiently comparable microstructures for the proposed mechanical comparison.
XRD peak broadening and pair-distribution-function measurements can quantify the degree of lattice distortion.
High-resolution TEM measurements of local strain fields can verify lattice distortion.
TEM measurements of dislocation density and behavior can help assess the proposed dislocation-mediated mechanism.
Heterogeneous internal stress fields produced by local lattice distortions impede dislocation motion.
Larger atomic-size mismatches make the proposed dislocation-impeding mechanism more pronounced.
Alloys with greater measured lattice distortion will have higher hardness than the low-distortion baseline.
Alloys with greater measured lattice distortion will have higher yield strength than the low-distortion baseline.
The strengthening effect will remain observable at room temperature and moderate elevated temperatures until thermal activation dominates dislocation dynamics.
A high-entropy alloy made from elements with comparable atomic radii will have relatively low lattice distortion while retaining high-entropy character.
The proposed relationship should hold in single-phase alloys without significant phase separation or precipitation.
Second phases may prevent the proposed lattice-distortion relationship from governing hardness and strength.
At sufficiently high temperatures, thermal softening may overwhelm strengthening associated with lattice distortion.
The quantitative contribution of lattice distortion relative to solid-solution and precipitation strengthening is uncertain.

Failure of increased measured lattice distortion to produce consistently higher hardness and yield strength, or attribution of strengthening to precipitation or phase changes, would falsify the hypothesis.
